facts.correction: The first formal/scheduled women's college basketball game was played on March 22, 1893 at Smith College, the class of 1895 (sophomores) beating the class of 1896 (freshmen) 5-4 in two 15-minute halves before an all-women crowd (no men admitted). Senda Berenson, hired at Smith in 1892, adapted Naismith's game and wrote the first set of women's basketball RULES (1892); she did not write the first women's rulebook — Clara Gregory Baer of Sophie Newcomb College published the first women's basketball rules BOOK in 1895 ('Basquette'). Berenson edited the first NATIONAL/official women's guide, published 1901 by Spalding's Athletic Library.
facts.note: Prior-claimant search run (superlative class). Core game facts hold at Tier 1: Smith's College Archivist (Nanci Young) confirms March 22, 1893 and the 5-4 sophomore win; the Naismith Hall confirms 1893 and 'no male spectators were even allowed'; the NCAA women's rules record book confirms Berenson read Naismith's 13 rules (published Jan 1892) and immediately created women's rules. TWO scope failures found. (1) 'wrote the first women's rulebook' is refuted by the NCAA record book's own 1894-95 entry: 'Clara Gregory Baer... publishes the first women's basketball rules book, calling her game Basquette.' Berenson's guide came out in 1901, six years later. (2) 'first college women's basketball game' needs its scope stated: Berenson's students were already playing informal in-class games at Smith in spring 1892, and the University of California women played an outside opponent (Miss Head's School, Berkeley) on Nov 18, 1892 — reported contemporaneously by Albert May in The San Francisco Call — which predates Smith's game by four months; the first women's INTERCOLLEGIATE game was Cal vs. Stanford, April 4, 1896. Wikipedia's own women's-basketball article concedes the Cal/Miss Head's priority, so the corpus dropped a caveat present in the index it cited. Safe phrasing for a card: 'the first formal, scheduled women's basketball game played at a college.'

facts.correction: Change '1891' to '1892': Senda Berenson (born Senda Valvrojenski, March 19, 1868, in Butrimonys, Vilna Governorate, Lithuania) emigrated to Boston as a child in 1875 and arrived at Smith College in 1892 for what was meant to be a temporary gymnastics post.
facts.note: Birth name, date and place hold: the Naismith Hall gives DOB March 19, 1868 and birthplace 'Vilna Governorate, LT' (Butrimonys sits in that governorate); the Jewish Women's Archive (Shalvi/Hyman Encyclopedia, signed by Ruth Gursky) gives 'born Senda Valvrojenski' and the 1875 emigration to Boston at age seven. 'Temporary post' is confirmed — the position opened because a Smith teacher fell ill, and Berenson was invited back only after her first year 'when her original, temporary position was made permanent.' The 1891 arrival date is the one bad detail: Smith College Libraries' own archival captions read 'Senda Berenson, Director of Physical Training, 1892-1911' (repeated four times), the 1941 Research Quarterly article on her is titled 'Director of Physical Education at Smith College, 1892-1911,' and Encyclopedia.com dates the hire to January 1892. Notably, Wikipedia — the source the corpus cited — never says 1891 anywhere in the article, so 1891 appears to be an interpolation rather than a copied error. This also removes an internal conflict with w-berenson-first-college-game-1893, which already said 1892.

facts.correction: Berenson introduced basketball at Smith in 1892 after reading Naismith's 13 rules, published in January 1892. The exact date of the first informal game is NOT known — informal in-class games were played in the spring of 1892; March 6, 1892 is the date a Smith student wrote a letter to her mother describing the new game as 'great fun.' The first formal interclass game was March 22, 1893, sophomores beating freshmen 5-4.
facts.note: 'An informal game was played March 6, 1892' is a misreading of the underlying source. Wikipedia's Berenson article — the corpus's own cited index — says explicitly: 'The exact date of the first informal game is not known, but one student wrote to her mother on March 6, 1892, describing a new game they were playing.' March 6, 1892 dates a LETTER, not a game. (It was also a Sunday, which fits a letter home and not a gym class.) Everything else holds at Tier 1: the NCAA women's rules record book dates Naismith's published 13 rules to January 1892 and says Berenson 'immediately creates new rules for women... and introduces basketball to smith women'; Smith's College Archivist confirms the March 22, 1893 game and the 5-4 sophomore win; the New York Herald reported five days after the game that 'the score was 5-4 in favor of the sophomores after a close contest of two 15-minute halves.' Recommend the corpus state 'spring 1892' for the informal games rather than a false-precision date.

All four rule elements confirmed twice at Tier 1, including against the PRIMARY DOCUMENT. The NCAA official women's basketball rules-history record book, 1891-92 entry: 'she divides the court into three equal sections and requires players to stay in their section. stealing the ball is prohibited, players may not hold the ball more than three seconds and there is a three-bounce limit on dribbles.' Berenson's own 1901 guide (Line Basket Ball, or Basket Ball for Women, Spalding's Athletic Library, full text on Internet Archive) states in her editorial: 'The two important changes are the division of the playing field and the prohibiting of snatching or batting the ball from the hands of another player'; 'a player should not be allowed to hold the ball longer than three seconds under penalty of a foul'; and 'not allowing the players to bounce the ball more than three consecutive times or lower than the knee.' One precision gain available to the corpus: the dribble rule also required the bounce be knee-high or higher, and the ban covered snatching OR batting the ball away. No refutation found.

facts.correction: Berenson edited 'Line Basket Ball, or Basket Ball for Women' (Spalding's Athletic Library, 1901), chaired the women's basketball rules committee from 1905 to 1917, and in 1985 was one of the FIRST THREE WOMEN enshrined in the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame — alongside Bertha Teague and Margaret Wade, all three in the Class of 1985. She was not the sole 'first woman.'
facts.note: This is the danger-class error the standard warns about. Prior-claimant search: Basketball-Reference's complete Hall of Fame register shows ZERO women in every class from 1959 through 1984 — so 1985 is correct as the year women first entered. But the Hall's own site lists Senda Berenson Abbott (Contributor), Bertha Teague (Contributor) and Margaret Wade (Coach) all as 'Enshrined 1985,' and the contemporaneous Christian Science Monitor report of July 5, 1985 is headlined 'Basketball Hall of Fame ushers in its FIRST WOMEN INDUCTEES' (plural) and states the three 'joined together in making history as the hall's first female enshrinees.' There is no documented ordering within a class, so any card asking 'who was the first woman in the Naismith Hall?' is unsafe as written — reframe as 'first women' or 'the 1985 class.' Sub-claims: the 1901 Spalding publication is confirmed by the NCAA record book ('these rules, edited by Berenson, are published in 1901 by spalding athletic library') and by the book itself on Internet Archive — note she was EDITOR, not sole author. The 1905-1917 chairmanship is corroborated by JWA (appointed 1905, served until 1917) and the Naismith Hall ('chaired the Women's Basketball Committee for twelve years' = 1905-17). 'Edited it for eighteen years' is the one soft detail — Wikipedia says eighteen years, JWA says she edited the rules through the 1916-17 issue; recommend the sourceable form '1901 until 1917' (medium confidence on '18').

facts.correction: Berenson's rules did NOT fix nine players a side. Her first official published rules (1901) allowed any number from FIVE TO TEN players per team on a court split into three zones, with a player limited to three dribbles (knee-high or higher) and three seconds holding the ball — written to make the game acceptable under Victorian ideas about women's exertion. Nine-a-side was one permitted option among six, not the original.
facts.note: Refuted directly by the primary document. In her own editorial in the 1901 guide Berenson writes: 'The original rules allow only five on a team. We have changed the rule to allow any number from five to ten players on a team.' The book carries six separate positional diagrams — 'Showing Position of Five on Team' through 'Ten on Team.' The NCAA official women's rules-history record book agrees independently: the 1901-02 entry says the committee adopted 'Berenson's original three-court rules... plus five to 10 players on a side'; 1903-04 narrowed it to 'six to nine players'; 1906-07 to 'five to nine.' So nine was never the fixed original. The claim traces to Wikipedia's women's-basketball article ('She increased participation to nine players per team'), which is Tier 3 and contradicted by two Tier-1 sources including Berenson herself. The zones / three dribbles / three seconds / Victorian-exertion framing all stand — only the player count is wrong.

facts.correction: Title IX was enacted June 23, 1972 as Pub. L. 92-318, title IX, sec. 901, 86 Stat. 373. Senator Birch Bayh of Indiana was its chief SENATE sponsor (Amendment 874 to S. 659, February 1972); Rep. Patsy Mink and Rep. Edith Green carried the House side, and the Act was renamed for Mink in 2002. The implementing regulation spelling out athletics compliance was signed by President Ford on May 27, 1975, published in June 1975, and took effect July 21, 1975 after the 45-day congressional review period expired.
facts.note: Enactment date verified Tier 1 at DOJ Civil Rights Division: 'Pub. L. 92-318, title IX, Sec. 901, June 23, 1972, 86 Stat. 373.' The '37 words' claim checks out arithmetically — I counted the statutory text of 20 U.S.C. 1681(a) as published by DOJ ('No person in the United States shall... receiving Federal financial assistance') and it is exactly 37 words. Bayh's role is documented Tier 1 by the Library of Congress Law Library research guide, which records his February 1972 Amendment 874 to S. 659 carrying the sex-discrimination provision through the Senate. Two fixes: (a) 'chiefly sponsored by' should be scoped to the Senate — the LOC guide gives Rep. Edith Green the House floor role and Mink is the statute's namesake, so an unqualified 'chief sponsor' card would be contestable; (b) the regulation chronology is sharper than 'not published until June 1975' — the Department of Education's own Policy Interpretation states it 'was signed by President Ford on May 27, 1975, and submitted to the Congress for review,' and 'became effective on July 21, 1975,' with a three-year compliance transition expiring July 21, 1978. June 1975 is the publication/congressional-transmittal month, so the original claim is not wrong, just imprecise.

facts.correction: Replace with Tier-1 numbers: girls' participation in US high school sports rose about TWELVEFOLD after Title IX — from 294,015 in 1971-72 (the first NFHS survey) to 3,539,596 in 2024-25. Basketball is the most widely offered women's college sport: the NCAA's Sports Sponsorship and Participation Rates Report shows women's basketball fielded by 99.0% of member institutions in 2018-19, more than any other women's sport. DROP the 'more than 450%' college-participation figure — it is not supportable from any Tier-1 baseline.
facts.note: Statistics are Tier-1-only and this fact cited Wikipedia for three of them; two do not survive. (1) 'Roughly ninefold' is REFUTED: the NFHS participation-survey history book gives 1971-72 girls = 294,015, and the NFHS 2024-25 release gives 3,539,596 — a ratio of 12.0, not 9. Ninefold matches roughly the 2001-02 level, so the number is two decades stale. This sub-claim is VOLATILE and needs a date anchor. (2) 'More than 450%' cannot be reproduced: the NCAA's own aggregate table gives women's championship-sport participation of 64,390 in 1981-82 rising to 218,496 in 2018-19, a +239% increase, and NCAA data does not extend back to 1972 for women (the AIAW era is outside its records). Any 450%-style figure depends on an unstated pre-NCAA baseline and should be dropped rather than re-sourced. (3) The basketball claim SURVIVES and is now Tier-1 anchored: from the NCAA women's sport-by-sport tables, 2018-19 overall sponsorship was basketball 99.0%, cross country 96.4%, volleyball 96.1%, soccer 93.3%, softball 89.7% — basketball is highest, so 'most widely offered' holds. The specific 98.8% figure is real but is the 2016-17 (and 2007-08) reading; it was 99.0% by 2018-19. Flag volatile.

facts.correction: American women played a divided-court game for nearly eighty years. The five-player, full-court game with a 30-second shot clock was permitted experimentally starting in 1969-70, ran a second experimental season, and was made the official rule for 1971-72 — about a year before Title IX (June 23, 1972). Drop 'and the first AIAW tournament': the 1972 national championship was held March 17-19, 1972 at Normal, Illinois (won by Immaculata) — the SAME season the rule took effect, roughly six months later, not a year — and national championships had already been held in 1969, 1970 and 1971 under the CIAW.
facts.note: Core claim verified at Tier 1 by the NCAA official women's rules-history record book, which is unusually explicit: 1969-70, 'experimental use of five-player, full-court game, in combination with 30-second clock, is permitted for the first time, continues for a second season, and is highly popular'; 1971-72, 'Five-player, full-court game and 30-second clock is made official, with little fanfare.' The 'nearly eighty years' framing checks out (Berenson's divided-court game 1892/93 to 1971 = 79 years). The trailing clause is where it slips. The NCAA women's record book's AIAW results table dates the 1972 National Basketball Championship to March 17-19, 1972 — inside the 1971-72 season, not a year later — and annotates it '$- DGWS Sponsored,' with 1969, 1970 and 1971 titles listed as '^- CIAW Sponsored' (1969 and 1970 flagged '%- Six Player Format'). So both 'one year before' and 'the first AIAW tournament' are loose. Title IX at ~12 months later is the only part of that clause that survives.

Verified at Tier 1, NCAA official women's basketball rules-history record book, 1984-85 entry: 'after two major research studies, committee legislates a smaller ball, about one inch less in circumference (becoming 28-1/2 to 29 inches) and two ounces lighter (18 to 20 ounces) than the previous ball. (this is the same weight recommended by the original women's committee in 1899.)' Effective for the 1984-85 season, i.e. adopted for play in the fall of 1984 as the corpus states. Two precision notes for whoever mines questions off this: (a) the rule set a legal RANGE of 28-1/2 to 29 inches, not a flat 28.5 — a card built on '28.5 inches' is fine, but a distractor set implying 29 inches is illegal would be wrong; (b) in 1984 the body that legislated it was the U.S. Girls' and Women's Basketball Rules Committee — formation of the NCAA Women's Basketball Rules Committee was not approved until the 1985 NCAA Convention — so 'the NCAA rules committee adopted it' would be a small anachronism. The weight change (two ounces lighter, to 18-20 oz) is an unused claim available in the same entry. No refutation found.

facts.correction: The three-point field goal came to women's college basketball as a one-year experiment in 1986-87 and was introduced as the official rule in 1987-88, set at 19 feet 9 inches from the center of the basket — the same distance NCAA men's basketball had adopted a year earlier, in 1986-87.
facts.note: Both halves confirmed at Tier 1 from the NCAA's own rules-history record books. Women's, 1987-88: 'three-point field goal is introduced and set at 19 feet, 9 inches from center of basket (after a year of experimentation).' Men's, 1986-87: 'the three-point field goal was introduced and set at 19 feet 9 inches from the center of the basket.' The distance and the one-year gap are right; the sentence construction is what breaks. As written — 'came to women's college basketball in 1986-87... the same distance the men's game had adopted a year earlier' — it implies the men adopted the line in 1985-86, which is false (1985-86 was the men's 45-second shot clock). Anchoring 'a year earlier' to the women's OFFICIAL date of 1987-88 makes the sentence true. Bonus verified claim from the same 1987-88 entry: men's and women's rules appeared in one rule book for the first time that season.

Both halves verified, and one Tier-1 source states them in a single sentence. FIBA's own site: 'The inaugural FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup was staged on March 7, 1953, in Santiago, Chile,' with 10 teams, and the USA beating hosts Chile 49-36 for the title. Olympedia (the Olympic statistical database of record) on Montreal 1976: 'The Olympic basketball program expanded in 1976, with women competing for the first time. Women had competed in World Championships since 1953, with the United States winning in 1953 and 1957, and the Soviet Union winning all the other tournaments, from 1959-75.' The 1976 women's tournament ran July 19-26 with 6 teams; Soviet Union gold, United States silver, Bulgaria bronze. The interval arithmetic is right: 1953 to 1976 is 23 years. Prior-claimant check for the 1953 'first' returned nothing earlier — FIBA itself calls it inaugural and the men's world championship (1950) is the only earlier FIBA world event. Rich unused claims sit here for question mining: host Santiago, the 49-36 final, two 16-minute halves, France's Anne Marie Golchen as leading scorer at 19.2 ppg, and the 1976 Olympic medal order.

facts.correction: The Edmonton Grads (1915-1940) were coached by J. Percy Page for the team's entire existence. Their traditional record is 502-20 in 522 games (96.2%) — the figure Canada Basketball still cites — but the City of Edmonton Archives, custodian of the Grads collection, puts it at 412-20 in 432 games (95.4%), and historian M. Ann Hall showed the 522 total folds in MacDougall Commercial high-school games from 1915-22. Either way it is roughly 95-96%. Scope the superlative to 'the best winning record in Canadian sport' / 'the best win rate of any women's sports team in North America' — NOT 'no basketball team at any level has matched.'
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. Coach: VERIFIED — TCE and CBC both have Page coaching the whole 25-year run ('For 25 years, the team's coach was J. Percy Page'). The STAT is genuinely contested between Tier-1 sources: Canada Basketball (national governing body) says '522 official games played, the Grads won 502 matches - a staggering winning percentage of 96.2%', while the City of Edmonton Archives online exhibit says 'They won 412 out of 432 games played, with only 20 losses.' TCE reconciles them: 'Traditionally, the Grads are considered to have played 522 games in total, winning 502 and losing only 20. However, these numbers have been challenged by M. Ann Hall, author of The Grads Are Playing Tonight! (2011). According to Hall, the Grads played over 400 games during their 25 years as a team, losing 20... the higher total (522) includes games played by the MacDougall Commercial junior and senior high school teams in the period from 1915 to 1922.' Hall is the named historian the standard itself cites for the Grads, so 502-20 cannot ship as bare fact. PRIOR-CLAIMANT SEARCH on 'no basketball team at any level has matched': REFUTED as written — the Harlem Globetrotters claim an all-time .987 (27,000+ wins). Their post-1950s games are exhibitions against a house opponent, so the comparison is soft, but no source asserts the Grads' figure as an all-basketball record; Canada's Sports Hall of Fame says 'unparalleled by any team in any sport, male or female' (unscoped puffery) and the City of Edmonton says only 'no other sporting team has a comparable record.' A t:4 question can safely ask '502-20' as the traditionally cited record if the stem says 'traditionally cited.'

dateChecked 2026-07-29. Two INDEPENDENT sources carry the quote verbatim: Canada Basketball (the national governing body) — 'Dr. James Naismith himself called the Grads "the finest basketball team that ever stepped out on a floor"' — and CBC News — 'Dr. James Naismith, the Canadian who invented the game of basketball, said the Grads were the "finest basketball team that ever stepped out on a floor."' The CBC piece is reported independently (it quotes M. Ann Hall and surviving Grad Kay MacBeth directly), so this is not one source wearing two hats. CAVEAT for question-writing: the occasion is NOT pinned down. Naismith's known, fully documented Grads text is a separate 1936 25th-anniversary letter reproduced by Canada's History ('Your record is without parallel in the history of basketball. There is no team that I mention more frequently in talking about the game...') which does NOT contain the 'finest... ever stepped out on a floor' line. So a card may attribute the quote to Naismith but must not date it or place it.

facts.correction: The Edmonton Grads played FSFI-arranged exhibition series alongside THREE Olympic Games — Paris 1924, Amsterdam 1928 and Berlin 1936 — and won all 24 games. They did travel to Los Angeles for the 1932 Games but never played there, because the IOC asked that non-Olympic sporting events be suspended during the Games. None of it counted: women's basketball was never even a demonstration sport before becoming an official Olympic event at Montreal 1976.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. The corpus claim is a hybrid no source supports: it takes 'four Olympics' from one lineage and '24 games' from another. Canada's History confronts the myth head-on: 'some say they were Olympic champions in 1924, 1928, 1932 and 1936. But women's basketball didn't become an Olympic sport until the Montreal Games in 1976, nor was it ever a demonstration sport at any prior Olympics... Although the Grads travelled to Los Angeles in 1932, they never hit the court there; this was because the IOC urged unnecessary sporting events to cease during the Games.' Same article: 'They also crossed the Atlantic Ocean three times and won every game against teams in Europe.' TCE independently: 'undefeated in 24 matches held in conjunction with the Olympic Summer Games in 1924, 1928 and 1936.' ECAMP (Edmonton Heritage Council) corroborates the LA trip from 1932 Edmonton Journal reporting: the Grads 'were headed to Los Angeles for the Olympics in a couple of months.' UNRESOLVED CONFLICT on the game count: Canada Basketball says 'the Grads attended four Olympics and won all 27 games they played.' 24 (three Games) vs 27 (four Games) is exactly the arithmetic you would expect if someone added a phantom 1932 series. I favour 24/three but confidence is medium — a question should ask 'which Olympics did they NOT play at' (LA 1932) rather than pin the game total. The 1976 Montreal date is independently solid in both TCE and Canada's History.

dateChecked 2026-07-29. Canada's History gives the mechanism and the date: Percy Page contacted Alice Milliat, whose Federation sportive feminine internationale invited the Grads to a tournament in Paris run alongside the 1924 men's Olympics; 'They played local teams in Paris, Strasbourg, Roubaix and Lille, defeating them all by lopsided scores. As a result, the Grads were given the undisputed right to the World's Basketball title by the FSFI.' ECAMP independently: 'The Grads had been national champs since 1922, North American champs since 1923, and World champs since 1924.' PRIOR-CLAIMANT SEARCH: no FSFI women's basketball world champion existed before 1924 (the FSFI itself was founded 1921 and this was its first basketball world title). The only competing claim is self-proclaimed — TCE records that the Cleveland Favorite-Knits turned up in 1923 already 'wearing shorts bearing the words "World Champs"' and the Grads beat them 53-33 on aggregate. Note CBC loosely writes that the Grads 'were declared world champions the next year [1923], after defeating a team from Cleveland' — that is the Underwood International Trophy / North American thread, a different title. The corpus already scopes the claim correctly to FSFI recognition; keep that scope in any question and do NOT shorten it to 'first world champions.'

facts.correction: The Grads disbanded in 1940 for several reasons at once: the Edmonton Arena, their home floor, was taken over for the Royal Canadian Air Force's Commonwealth Air Training Program; wartime travel restrictions cancelled competition in Canada, the United States and Europe; attendance had fallen (few teams were good enough to give them a game, and fans could now hear sport on radio); and coach Percy Page was elected to the Alberta legislature in 1940.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. All three reasons the corpus names are individually supported, but it presents an incomplete list as complete and glosses one causal link as its own inference. TCE: 'There were several reasons for this decision, including the loss of their arena, which had been taken over by the government for the Air Force Commonwealth Training Program. Wartime conditions made travel difficult and led to the cancellation of many competitions in Canada, the United States and in Europe; moreover, there were few teams good enough to compete with the Grads. Finally, attendance at games had declined; and, in 1940, Page was elected to the provincial government.' Canada Basketball names the service explicitly: 'the Grads' home Edmonton Arena was repurposed by the Royal Canadian Air Force and the team was disbanded' — so the corpus's 'RCAF took over the Edmonton Arena' is right, it is the BCATP/Air Force Commonwealth Training Program. Canada's History adds radio and dates the last game: June 5, 1940, before 6,000+ fans at the Edmonton Arena, vs the Chicago Queen Anne Aces (Provincial Archives of Alberta captions the final-game photo 'Queen Anne Candies' — the club name varies by source, so don't build a card on the opponent's exact name). The corpus's 'attendance had fallen BECAUSE nobody could give them a game' fuses two separate reasons the sources list independently; and it omits Page's election, which every Canadian source treats as a real factor.

facts.correction: The All American Red Heads were founded in 1936 in Cassville, Missouri by C. M. 'Ole' Olson and are the longest-running professional women's basketball franchise in the sport's history (the Naismith Hall of Fame's own wording) — commonly called America's first, and 42 years ahead of the WBL. Every player wore red hair, dyed if necessary: Olson's wife Doyle owned a chain of beauty parlors that the team originally publicized.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. VERIFIED at Tier 1: hoophall.com — 'Formed in 1936... Owners C.M. Olson and Orwell Moore' — and Encyclopedia of Arkansas (CALS, peer-reviewed, sourced to Molina and to Moore/Harrison) — 'formed in 1936 in Cassville, Missouri, with Connie Mack Olson as its founder and coach. Originally, the team, all sporting dyed or natural red hair, publicized Olson's Beauty Parlors.' Beauty-salon ownership: APBR (specialist org) says the name came from 'the chain of beauty salons owned by Olson's wife's' and America Comes Alive names her — 'Olson's wife, Doyle, owned five beauty parlors in Arkansas and Missouri.' Two independent, and this is a soft/cultural claim where Tier 2 suffices; note EOA locates the parlors in Kansas and Missouri, so don't put the states on a card. SUPERLATIVE 'first professional women's basketball team in the United States' — this is the weak link and the reason for the fix. I ran the prior-claimant search and could not surface a documented earlier US women's PRO team, but neither of the two strongest sources will say 'first': the Naismith Hall says they 'remain the longest-running women's professional franchise in the history of basketball'; the AAU calls them 'among the first professional women's basketball teams'; Arkansas Times calls them 'the first women's barnstorming basketball team and the last standing.' When a Hall of Fame writes around a superlative, that is a signal. Ship the 'longest-running' form, which is Tier-1 and airtight. Also: 'forty years before the WBL' is 42 (WBL tipped off 1978).

facts.correction: Keep: the All American Red Heads barnstormed for fifty years, 1936 to 1986, playing MEN'S teams by MEN'S rules, upwards of 200 games a season. DROP 'more than 60,000 miles a year, October through May' — it traces only to Wikipedia. If a travel/schedule detail is wanted, the sourced version is Arkansas Times' 'up to 220 games a year' and a season of roughly seven months.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. Core claims VERIFIED at Tier 1 — hoophall.com: 'Formed in 1936, the all-female five played men's teams by men's rules... The Red Heads played upwards of 200 games in a single season from coast to coast.' Fifty-year span confirmed twice independently: Missouri Sports Hall of Fame — 'in 1936, businessman C.M. "Ole" Olson started a barnstorming women's basketball team... the organization would last a whopping 50 years through 1986' — and Encyclopedia of Arkansas, whose WBHOF exhibit description covers 'the team's history from 1936 to 1986' and which explains the only thing that could confuse the end date: a single commemorative reunion game on July 26, 1996 vs the Walmart All Stars, 'following a ten-year interval.' So 1986 is the real end. REFUTATION ATTEMPT on the mileage: I could not find '60,000 miles' or 'October through May' in the Naismith HOF page, Encyclopedia of Arkansas, Missouri Sports HOF, APBR, America Comes Alive, or the Arkansas Times cover story. Every hit resolves to Wikipedia's sentence ('Seasons ran from October to late April or early May and consisted of approximately 200 games, traveling over 60,000 miles by car') or a copy of it — Tier 3 alone, which never ships. A former player quoted in the America Comes Alive comments says 'almost 7 months a season,' which is consistent with Oct-to-April but is testimony, not a record.

facts.correction: The All American Red Heads were enshrined as a TEAM in the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2012 — the first women's team ever enshrined there. The 2011 Women's Basketball Hall of Fame honour was NOT an induction: the WBHOF recognised them with its 'Trailblazers of the Game' award, a separate honour given to teams, leagues and organisations.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. Naismith 2012 is Tier-1 airtight: hoophall.com's team page reads 'TEAM / All American Red Heads / Enshrined 2012' and its By The Numbers panel says '2012 — First women's team enshrined in the Basketball Hall of Fame.' Encyclopedia of Arkansas independently: 'In 2012, the Red Heads became the first women's basketball team inducted into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame.' Arkansas Times dates the ceremony to Sept. 7, 2012 in Springfield and records that historian John Molina first nominated them in 2006 and applied six times. THE 2011 CLAIM IS WHERE THE CORPUS IS WRONG. The WBHOF's own member directory has no Red Heads entry (wbhof.com/member/all-american-red-heads returns 404, while wbhof.com/member/hazel-walker resolves fine), and its Trailblazers page — the one that carries this honour — is currently 404 on the live site, with the Wayback copy blocked to me, so I could not read the primary text directly. Search snippets of that WBHOF page consistently describe 'Trailblazers of the Game' as an award for 'teams, leagues and/or organizations' and place the Red Heads at the June 11, 2011 ceremony as a recognition/display, not an enshrinement. Corroborating negative evidence: the Arkansas Times 2012 cover story recounts the team's WBHOF relationship as a 1999 exhibit ('When the Women's Basketball Hall of Fame opened in Knoxville in 1999, it included a Red Heads exhibit, complete with the team's trademark white limousine') and treats Naismith 2012 as the breakthrough — it never mentions a 2011 WBHOF induction, which a cover story would not omit. Confidence medium only because I could not load the WBHOF page itself; the Naismith half is high.

facts.correction: In 1949 Hazel Walker founded Hazel Walker's Arkansas Travelers, becoming the first woman to start and own her own professional basketball team — and, per the Encyclopedia of Arkansas, the only woman ever to own, manage and star for one. The Travelers played only men's teams, by men's rules, averaged 220 games a season, and won 80 to 85 percent of them across sixteen seasons from 1949 to 1965.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. Nearly all of this survives, at Tier 1. facts.correction: Before the Olympic track medals and the golf majors, Babe Didrikson was a basketball player: an AAU All-American in each of her three seasons, 1930 through 1932, for the Employers Casualty Company's Golden Cyclones of Dallas, whom she led to the 1931 AAU national championship — beating the Wichita Thurstons 28-26 on a Didrikson basket in the last 30 seconds. Replace 'her secretarial job was a formality so she could play as an amateur' with the accurate mechanism: the company put her on the payroll doing office work, which is what kept her an amateur under the AAU industrial-league system.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. Everything substantive checks out on two independent Tier-2 sources. Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas: 'Didrikson was recruited during her senior year in 1930 to do office work at Employers Casualty Insurance Company of Dallas and to spark the company's semiprofessional women's basketball team, the Golden Cyclones. Between 1930 and 1932 she led the team to two finals and a national championship and was voted All-American each season.' The Babe Didrikson Zaharias Foundation independently pins the years: 'named All-American in 1930, 1931, & 1932.' THE 1931 TITLE YEAR — which TSHA leaves undated — is nailed by ProHoopsHistory (Curtis M. Harris, historian, writing from contemporaneous newspapers): the Cyclones beat Crescent College 42-27 in the semifinal, then 'The Golden Cyclones won the AAU national title by a score of 28-26' over the Wichita Thurstons, 'thanks to a Didrikson basket in the game's final 30 seconds.' Cross-checks against the AAU champions roll (1931: Dallas Golden Cyclones over Wichita Thurstons) and against 1932, when the Cyclones lost the final to Oklahoma Presbyterian College 35-32. THE ONE THING I FIXED is 'a formality.' The job was real and paid: ProHoopsHistory documents $75/month raised to $90 in 1932, and TSHA has her actually doing office work. The honest framing is that AAU industrial-league employment is what preserved amateur standing — 'technically, these players weren't professionals because they were paid to work at a company.' Also flagging for the merge step, not a fact error: this record is tagged league 'wnba', which is wrong for a 1930s AAU player. dateChecked 2026-07-29. QUARANTINE, not deletion — obscure, not false. The whole fact rests on one Tier-3 table, and the sources that do exist actively disagree with each other. facts.correction: Nera White was a 15-time AAU All-American who led Nashville Business College to ten national championships between 1955 and 1969 and was named MVP of the AAU national tournament ten times. She was widely called the greatest woman ever to play the game, and in 1992 she and Lusia Harris-Stewart became the first women enshrined in the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame as PLAYERS — three women had already been enshrined in 1985: Senda Berenson Abbott as a contributor and Bertha Teague and Margaret Wade as coaches.
facts.note: dateChecked 2026-07-29. HIGH STAKES — playable card AND a 'first' claim, and the 'first' is WRONG AS WRITTEN. The Naismith Hall's own member pages (Tier 1) show Senda Berenson Abbott (CONTRIBUTOR), Bertha Teague (COACH) and Margaret Wade (COACH) all enshrined in 1985 — seven years before White — and its Nera White page lists Lusia Harris-Stewart in the same Class of 1992. So the safe phrasing is 'first women enshrined as players, jointly with Lusia Harris-Stewart, 1992' — never 'the first woman inducted.' EVERYTHING ELSE IS AIRTIGHT AT TIER 1. The two halls differ only on the window (WBHOF 1955-1969 = her career; Naismith 1958-1969 = when the ten titles actually fell) — reconcilable, not a conflict, but a question must not ask 'in what year did White win her first NBC title' expecting 1955. ACTIVE REFUTATION ATTEMPT: both NCAA.com's 2022 obituary and Delta State's athletics HOF listing print '2,891' in one place — a digit transposition. 2,981 is right: it is what the NCAA record book, the Naismith Hall and Delta State's own Trailblazers feature all carry, and only 2,981 is arithmetically consistent with 25.9 ppg over 115 games (2,891/115 = 25.1). facts.correction: Drop the '1,060 points' season total, or flag it low-confidence, until a Tier-1 season total is found — the statistics rule is Tier-1 only and I could not source it above Wikipedia. Everything else holds. Suggested restatement: "In 1975-76 Lusia Harris led the nation in scoring at 31.2 points a game, including a 58-point game against Tennessee Tech."

The Naismith Hall independently corroborates the average: 'In 1976 alone, the bruising center averaged 31.2 points and 15.1 rebounds per game.' The 1,060 figure is arithmetically plausible (Delta State went 33-1 that season = 34 games; 31.2 x 34 = 1,060.8) but plausible is not sourced, and the NCAA's pre-NCAA record book publishes no season-total table for this era. Every component checks. Montreal 1976 was the first Olympic women's basketball tournament (Olympedia: 'Basketball, Women — Date 19-26 July 1976 — the first Olympic basketball tournament for women in 1976'), so a prior claimant is impossible by construction. Basketball-Reference confirms the opponent and date: Mon, Jul 19, 1976, United States 71, Japan 84. Olympedia's final table confirms the medals — Soviet Union gold, United States silver, Bulgaria bronze — and shows Harris ('Lucy Harris') leading the USA with 76 points (15.2/g) and 35 rebounds. RESIDUAL DOUBT, recorded honestly: Basketball-Reference shows THREE games on July 19 (Czechoslovakia-Bulgaria, USA-Japan, Canada-Soviet Union) and I could not find any published schedule with tip-off times establishing which tipped first. NBA.com asserts USA-Japan was the tournament's first game; no source contradicts it. Confidence set to medium for that ordering only — the rest of the fact is high. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft page (fetched via curl with a browser UA — it 403s WebFetch) has the row exactly: Round 7, pick 137 overall, NOJ, Lusia Harris, Delta State University. Prior-claimant search on 'only woman ever officially drafted': the San Francisco Warriors selected Denise Long in 1969 and the NBA blocked the pick ('the NBA blocked it because she didn't meet the criteria to be drafted — in part because of her gender', NBA.com); Long appears nowhere on Basketball-Reference's 1969 draft page, which is what makes 'officially' the correct qualifier. hoophall's By-The-Numbers panel states 'Only — Woman Drafted by the NBA'. The Naismith Hall's Harris page lists both facts as discrete By-The-Numbers entries: '3x AIAW National Champion' and '3x AIAW Tournament MVP'. The NCAA's official AIAW results table independently confirms the three title years (Delta St. 1975, 1976, 1977). Delta State Athletics states 'Harris... was the AIAW tournament MVP three times' and its HOF listing records 'Most Valuable Player 1974-77'. Delta State's game accounts also name her tournament MVP in 1975 and 1976 specifically. Nothing contradicts. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

facts.correction: Two fixes. (1) 'the NCAA began sponsoring women's basketball and absorbed it' is wrong — the NCAA did not absorb the AIAW. The AIAW sued the NCAA under the Sherman Act (filed Oct 9, 1981), closed business June 30, 1982, lost at trial (AIAW v. NCAA, 558 F. Supp. 487, D.D.C. 1983) and lost on appeal (735 F.2d 577, D.C. Cir. 1984). Restate as: '...until 1982, when it ceased operations after the NCAA began offering its own women's championships; its antitrust suit against the NCAA failed.' (2) The division history should read: a separate Small College tournament was added in 1975 and was split into Division II and Division III in 1980 (the NCAA table's own headings: 'Small College Tournament 1975-1979', 'Division II 1980-1982', 'Division III 1980-1982'). DROP or mark low-confidence the 'plus a junior/community college division' clause — see note.
facts.note: The 1972-1982 span and 'eleven tournaments' are confirmed by the NCAA's official AIAW results table. The junior/community college division clause fails the source standard on a bounded lookup: it appears only on Wikipedia, which carries no footnote for it, and it is absent from the NCAA record book entirely. There is circumstantial support (Francis Marion University's page confirms Pearl Moore played at Anderson Junior College in fall 1975, and Wikipedia lists Anderson as the 1974-77 junior/community college champion) but that is Tier 3 corroborating Tier 3. Also worth a scope note: the AIAW itself was founded in 1971, and the NCAA record book flags the 1972 tournament as DGWS-sponsored ('$- DGWS Sponsored'), with 1969-71 predecessors run by the CIAW. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

Checked line-by-line against the NCAA's official AIAW CHAMPIONSHIP RESULTS table and it matches exactly: 1972 Immaculata, 1973 Immaculata, 1974 Immaculata, 1975 Delta St., 1976 Delta St., 1977 Delta St., 1978 UCLA, 1979 Old Dominion, 1980 Old Dominion, 1981 Louisiana Tech, 1982 Rutgers. Eleven tournaments, six programs — both counts correct. This is an 'every X' superlative, so scope matters and the fact should say so: this is the Division I / Large College line ONLY. The same NCAA table also lists CIAW-sponsored predecessor champions (1969 West Chester, 1970 Cal St. Fullerton, 1971 Mississippi-Women) and entirely separate Small College (1975-79), Division II (1980-82) and Division III (1980-82) champion lines — so 'every AIAW champion' without the Division I qualifier would be false. The fact's existing wording ('Every AIAW Division I champion') already carries the qualifier correctly. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

All five scores match the NCAA's official AIAW results table character-for-character: 1972 Immaculata 52-48 West Chester; 1973 Immaculata 59-52 Queens (NY); 1974 Immaculata 68-53 Mississippi Col.; 1975 Delta St. 90-81 Immaculata; 1976 Delta St. 69-64 Immaculata. The 'five straight championship games' claim is independently confirmed by the Naismith Hall's Cathy Rush page, whose By-The-Numbers panel reads '5x AIAW National Championship Game appearances' (and '6x Final Four appearances' — the sixth Final Four is 1977, where Immaculata lost the semifinal to LSU 74-68 and finished fourth). The runner-up in 1974 is correctly 'Mississippi College', a distinct school from 'Mississippi-Women' (the 1971 CIAW champion) — an easy confusion this fact avoids. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

facts.correction: Two fixes. (1) '1972 to 1977' is wrong — Rush coached Immaculata from 1970 to 1977. The Naismith Hall: 'She began her coaching career at Immaculata College in 1970, less than two years after graduating from West Chester University... Her stint at the small Catholic school for women lasted only seven seasons' (1970-71 through 1976-77 = seven). 1972 is the year of her first title, not her first season. (2) 'the 2009 film' is at best ambiguous — The Mighty Macs was completed in 2009 but did not reach theaters until October 21, 2011 (Freestyle Releasing). Say 'the film The Mighty Macs (completed 2009, released theatrically in 2011)' or simply 'the 2011 film'.
facts.note: Everything else verified at Tier 1. 'No gym of its own' — Naismith Hall: 'Lacking even the luxury of a homecourt, the Mighty Macs won three consecutive AIAW national championships beginning in 1972', and the Immaculata team page adds 'a small suburban school that lacked a homecourt, athletic scholarships, and even the most basic of equipment.' 'Five consecutive national finals' confirmed by the Hall's '5x AIAW National Championship Game appearances' and by the NCAA results table (finals 1972-76). Immaculata is in Malvern, PA, in Chester County outside Philadelphia — correct. OPTIONAL ENRICHMENT available from the same Tier-1 page: her career coaching record was 149-15, she was AMF-Voit Coach of the Year in 1973 and 1974, and her 1975 team played Maryland in the first nationally televised women's game. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

Verified, and the superlative is if anything UNDERSTATED. Rutgers Athletics (Tier 1, her employer): 'When Theresa Shank Grentz was hired at Rutgers in August of 1976, she became the first full-time women's basketball coach in the nation' — so 'first full-time paid women's coach at Rutgers' is true but holds in a wider scope than claimed; recommend upgrading the wording to the national scope that the Tier-1 source actually supports. Grentz coached Rutgers 19 seasons (434-150) and then Illinois (WBHOF: 'St. Joseph's (two years), Rutgers (19 years), and Illinois (six years)'), and WBHOF confirms she 'was a member of the Mighty Macs' three AIAW national championship squads (1972, 1973, 1974)'. Marianne Crawford Stanley played on Immaculata's 1973 and 1974 title teams and the NCAA's official AIAW table lists her as head coach of the Old Dominion champions in BOTH 1979 and 1980; she also coached Cal and USC as claimed (her full head-coaching line is Old Dominion, Penn, USC, Stanford, California — the corpus list is incomplete, not wrong). ONE SOURCE CONFLICT recorded but not load-bearing here: WBHOF says Grentz 'took the reins at Rutgers in 1975' while Rutgers Athletics says August 1976. Rutgers' own record should win; the corpus fact states no year, so nothing to fix. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

Every element matches the NCAA's official AIAW results table: 1975 Delta St. 90-81 over Immaculata, 1976 Delta St. 69-64 over Immaculata (Immaculata twice, as claimed), 1977 Delta St. 68-55 over LSU (the 68-55 score is exact). Harris as tournament MVP all three years is carried by the Naismith Hall's '3x AIAW Tournament MVP' entry and by Delta State Athletics. Margaret Wade is correctly the coach of record for all three in the NCAA table. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

Both scores are exact in the NCAA's official AIAW results table: '1979 Old Dominion / Marianne Stanley / Louisiana Tech / 75-65 / Greensboro, NC' and '1980 Old Dominion / Marianne Stanley / Tennessee / 68-53 / Mt. Pleasant, MI'. Back-to-back confirmed. Nancy Lieberman's presence for both title seasons is confirmed by the same NCAA record book's pre-NCAA career records, which list 'Nancy Lieberman, Old Dominion 1977-80, 134 G, 2,430 Pts, 1,167 Rebs' — NCAA notation 1977-80 covers 1976-77 through 1979-80, spanning both championship years. 'At the point' is a position description rather than a stat; Olympedia lists her as a guard on the 1976 US Olympic team and she is universally described as ODU's point guard. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

facts.correction: Scope the superlative. Mercy, both in the NCAA table) and ran championships in other sports through June 1982. In the championship game at the Palestra in Philadelphia, MVP Patty Coyle scored a career-high 30 points while Dorner added in 25.' The NCAA's official AIAW table confirms Rutgers over Texas at Philadelphia but prints no score for this game, which is why the Rutgers page carries it. facts.correction: The attribution of the 4,061 is wrong. 4,061 is Pearl Moore's TOTAL college career; only 3,884 of it came at Francis Marion. Francis Marion University Athletics (Tier 1): 'Moore started her collegiate career at Anderson Junior College in the fall of 1975. After one semester at Anderson (eight games and 177 points), she transferred to Francis Marion... The 5-7 guard-forward went on to score 3,884 points in a Patriot uniform. Her career point total includes the points scored at Anderson, because at that time in women's basketball, two- and four-year schools regularly competed against each other and all results counted.' The NCAA's own pre-NCAA record book independently lists 'Pearl Moore, Francis Marion 1975-79, 127 G, 1,620 FG, 644 FT, *3,884 Pts, 30.6 Avg' — 3,884, not 4,061 (3,884 + 177 = 4,061 exactly). Restate as: 'Pearl Moore scored 4,061 points in her college career — 3,884 at Francis Marion from 1975 to 1979 plus 177 in eight games at Anderson Junior College — averaging 30.6 a game at Francis Marion.'
facts.note: The superlative survives a real prior-claimant search and should be kept, scoped. The Naismith Hall's By-The-Numbers panel states outright '4,061 — Women's College Basketball All-Time Leader in Points'. Francis Marion runs the prior-claimant check for us: 'she still stands as the only female player to reach 4,000 career points. Miriam Walker-Samuels of Claflin College (SC) is second on the women's scoring list with 3,855 points.' Caitlin Clark finished 2024 with 3,951, which is the NCAA Division I record and sits below 4,061; no one has passed 4,061 as of 2026-07-29. 'Four-time AIAW Small College All-American' is confirmed by the Naismith Hall ('4x AIAW Small College All-America'). 'Averaging over 30 a game' is confirmed at 30.6 by both the NCAA record book and FMU. SEPARATE CAUTION for any future fact built on her 60-point game: the Naismith Hall page says the 60 came 'against the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga', but Francis Marion's own record says the 60 came against Eastern Washington State in the 1978 AIAW Small College National Tournament (114-71) and that the UT-Chattanooga game (Mar 10, 1979) was her 42-point finale. Trust the school. dateChecked 2026-07-29.

Prior-claimant search run: professional women's TEAMS predate the WBL by four decades (All-American Red Heads, 1936, Naismith HOF; Hazel Walker's Arkansas Travelers, 1949) but APBR's compiled history of women's pro basketball shows no US women's pro LEAGUE before the WBL - every rival league (LPBA 1980, WABA 1984, NWBA 1986, LBA 1991, WBA 1993) came after; three seasons fall 1978 to spring 1981 and 19 years before the WNBA (1997) both check out; recommend the fact keep its explicit 'league / in the United States' scope so it is not read as 'first women's pro basketball'.

Two independent Tier-2s: The IX/The Next (Kiri Oler, citing NYT/Washington Post/UPI) gives the draft as July 18, 1978 at the Essex House in Manhattan with Byrne as founder, and the Handbook of Texas (Debbie Mauldin Cottrell) independently gives 'founded in the fall of 1978 by William Byrne' with eight teams; APBR's franchise chronology confirms the eight 1978-79 charter clubs.

APBR's playoff results give Houston over Iowa in five (1 May 79, 111-104), New York over Iowa 3-1 (9 Apr 80) and Nebraska over Dallas 3-2 (20 Apr 81); Handbook of Texas independently confirms Houston's 1979 title, so three champions, one apiece.

The $50,000 charter franchise fee is solid (The IX citing contemporaneous press; Karra Porter's Mad Seasons references owners putting down $50,000), but the $14 million loss figure traces to a single source - commissioner Dave Almstead's November 1981 announcement as reported by the NYT, 23 Nov 1981 - which is Tier 1 but paywalled and could not be read directly, hence medium.

Karra Porter's Mad Seasons independently confirms both numbers I most doubted - 'cheered by 7,824 people in the stands' and 'Waddy-Rossow was the game's high scorer with 30 points and 12 rebounds' - while the Handbook of Texas and WNBA.com confirm Dec 9, 1978, Milwaukee, Chicago 92-87; the arena is the Milwaukee Arena, also known then as the MECCA.

Naismith Hall (Tier 1) lists Houston Angels as Harris-Stewart's only pro team; ESPN and NBA.com independently date that stint to 1979-80 as her only professional season; The IX quotes her 1978 refusal ('I wouldn't even consider playing for that salary') over the $3,000-$5,000 range - worth noting the estimate came from the Minnesota franchise and she sat out 1978-79 rather than declining outright forever.

APBR and Fun While It Lasted both list Easterling (Chicago Hustle) as 1978-79 MVP and 1978-79 All-Star Game MVP; contemporaneous Newsday and NY Daily News clips (14 Mar 1979 game at the Felt Forum) confirm East 112-99, 2,731 fans and Easterling's 19 points/18 assists MVP - superlative scope is 'the WBL's first-season MVP', and note the piquant detail that she won All-Star MVP for the LOSING side (the Midwest squad).

facts.correction: Pearl Moore scored 27 in the clincher, not 22. Corrected fact: 'The WBL's three champions: the Houston Angels over the Iowa Cornets in 1978-79, the New York Stars over Iowa in 1979-80 (clinching game four 125-114 on April 9, 1980 behind 27 points from Pearl Moore and 22 from Janice Thomas, with Molly Bolin scoring 36 in defeat), and the Nebraska Wranglers over the Dallas Diamonds in 1980-81.'
facts.note: The only surviving game account - the UPI box score in the NYT, 10 Apr 1980, cited on the New York Stars (WBL) page - has Moore 27 and Thomas 22, so '22 points each' is wrong; APBR confirms the 125-114 score and that it was game four of a 3-1 series; medium because the NYT/UPI box is paywalled and read only via its citation.

Two lines of evidence: AP via NYT (21 Apr 1981) as cited, and Fun While It Lasted drawing on Karra Porter's Mad Seasons, which gives Walker's line as 12-of-16 from the floor and 15-of-17 from the stripe for 39 in the deciding fifth game at Omaha Civic Auditorium (Nebraska 99-90, per APBR); the 'less than half her season average' clause survives the arithmetic check - Lieberman averaged 26.3 ppg in 1980-81, so 12 is under half - but that average is only Tier-2 sourced, hence medium.

AP via NYT (22 Mar 1981) reported the walkout and suspension the next morning; Karra Porter has commissioner Sherwin Fischer's own account of the 21 Mar 1981 night ('we played the Star Spangled Banner, the teams lined up, and just as they lined up, they paraded out to the parking lot, with me in hot pursuit') and Fischer suspended coach Terry Kunze and eight players indefinitely, calling it 'very detrimental to the league'; the game was a road game at Chicago, which the players chose because the league office was there.

All five sub-claims hold: WNBA.com's own release names Orender president (Feb 2005; she played WBL for the Stars, Gems and Hustle), the Mercury's release and FIBA's Hall of Fame page both have Meyers as GM from Sept 2006, Blazejowski was the Liberty's first VP/GM (named 7 Jan 1997, stepped down 2010 per ESPN), Lieberman was Detroit's first head coach/GM in 1998, and McGraw joined the California Dreams partway through 1979-80 before her Notre Dame tenure.

Fun While It Lasted, sourcing Karra Porter's Mad Seasons, states the 1979-80 expansion clubs cost $100,000 'up from $50,000 for the league's charter franchises a year before', matching The IX's $50,000; the repeated $14 million loss figure again rests solely on the paywalled NYT report of Almstead's Nov 1981 announcement, so medium.

facts.correction: The league did not double and the Washington Metros were not an addition. Corrected fact: 'The WBL grew from eight teams to fourteen in three divisions for its second season, 1979-80, adding six expansion franchises - the California Dreams, Dallas Diamonds, New Orleans Pride, Philadelphia Fox, St. Louis Streak and San Francisco Pioneers - while the Dayton Rockettes relocated to become the Washington Metros. Both the Fox and the Metros folded before the season ended.'
facts.note: APBR's franchise chronology explicitly tags six 1979-80 clubs '[expansion franchise]' and the Washington Metros '[formerly Dayton Rockettes]', and the Handbook of Texas independently says the league 'increased to fourteen teams across three divisions' - 8 to 14 is not doubling, and listing Washington as an addition double-counts a relocated charter club.

facts.correction: The division name is wrong. Corrected fact: 'The WBL's original eight: Chicago Hustle, Iowa Cornets, Milwaukee Does and Minnesota Fillies in the Midwest Division; Dayton Rockettes, Houston Angels, New Jersey Gems and New York Stars in the Eastern Division.'
facts.note: The eight team names are confirmed by APBR and the Handbook of Texas, but APBR's 1978-79 standings head the non-Eastern group 'Midwest Division', and the March 1979 All-Star Game was contested as East vs Midwest (Doug Bruno coaching the Midwest) - 'Western Division' appears on Wikipedia and is probably bleed-through from 1979-80, when a genuine Western Division (Houston, San Francisco, California, Dallas) existed; medium because the two secondary sources disagree and no 1978 media guide was reachable.

This is an interpretive causal claim, not a datum: it traces to a single 1981 NYT piece written by Donna Chait Geils - i.e. WBL player and future WNBA president Donna Orender, a firsthand participant - saying Byrne founded the league expecting the 1980 Olympics to showcase its stars and that the US-led boycott 'only added to the league's misfortunes'; Mad Seasons corroborates the boycott's concrete effect on WBL-bound players (Blazejowski, Nissen). Verified as a sourced judgment with medium confidence, not as a measured cause.

APBR and FWIL both list 1979-80 MVP as SHARED between Bolin (Iowa) and Ann Meyers, and the Naismith Hall's Meyers page independently records '1980 WBL Co-MVP' - so 'a WBL Most Valuable Player' is true but the fact would read better as co-MVP. 'Set the league's lasting scoring records' is the publisher's own framing of Mad Seasons and is safe only because the WBL folded, freezing its records (55 points on 2 Mar 1980 is the single-game mark); flagged medium because secondary sources disagree on WHICH season she averaged 32.8 (1979-80 with Iowa vs 1980-81 with San Francisco) - do not mint a question on that average until a Tier-1 season line is found.

University of Iowa Libraries' archival authority record (Tier 1 institutional): 'In 1978 Bolin was the first player to sign with the Women's Basketball League (WBL)', and Karra Porter states it independently and more precisely: 'In March 1978 Molly Bolin became the first player to sign a contract in the Women's Professional Basketball League.' Prior-claimant check passes on chronology - she signed months before the July 18, 1978 draft, and no earlier WBL signing surfaced; note the month conflict in secondary retellings (March per Porter, June per Iowa Capital Dispatch), so the corpus fact is right to state no date.

Robin Herman's NYT report of 19 Jul 1978 (as cited) has her announcing from a national-team tour that she would stay amateur for the 1980 Olympics; The IX confirms she declined to sign and that Mad Seasons adds the corroborating detail that she donated her Superstars prize Corvette to USA Basketball to protect her amateur standing and got it back after the boycott; she was Liberty VP/GM from Jan 1997 to 2010. One honest gap: she DID eventually play in the WBL, joining the New Jersey Gems for the 1980-81 final season - the fact's 'turned down the WBL' is true only for 1978-80 and should say so.

Naismith Hall (Tier 1) calls her 'the first woman player drafted into the Women's Basketball League' and The IX names her the first overall pick by Houston at the 18 Jul 1978 Essex House draft; the co-MVP half is confirmed three ways (Naismith '1980 WBL Co-MVP', FIBA 'Co-MVP ... of the WBL in 1979-1980', APBR co-MVP with Bolin) and FIBA/Naismith list New Jersey Gems as her only pro club - she never played for Houston, which the fact correctly does not claim. Caution for question-writing: FIBA also calls her WBL 'Top Scorer' in 1979-80, which conflicts with Bolin leading the league - do not use that.

facts.correction: Lieberman was the WBL's ROOKIE OF THE YEAR for 1980-81, not its MVP: as a rookie with the Dallas Diamonds she averaged 26.3 points and made the All-Pro first team, and the 1980-81 WBL Most Valuable Player was Rosie Walker of the champion Nebraska Wranglers (26.0 ppg, 14.4 rpg). 1980-81 was correctly identified as the WBL's third and final season - the league disbanded after it.
facts.note: SOURCE CONFLICT worth Aaron's attention: hoophall.com's Lieberman bio blurb says 'Earning WBL MVP honors with the Dallas Diamonds in 1981', but the contemporaneous record (Omaha World-Herald award report cited by the 1980-81 WBL season page, Fun While It Lasted's WBL trophy case) and the Jewish Women's Archive encyclopedia all have her as Rookie of the Year with Rosie Walker as MVP - HOF prose blurbs are not a record of fact.

Tier-1 (Women's Basketball HOF) confirms every element except one: silver at 18 in 1976 (youngest basketball medallist in Olympic history), back-to-back ODU AIAW titles 1979-1980, the only two-time Wade Trophy winner, and 'number one draft choice of the Dallas Diamonds of the WBL in 1980'; Naismith HOF and APBR confirm Dallas won the 1984 WABA title (one-season league). The 1984 WABA MVP is the one claim with no Tier-1 behind it - it rests on Tier-2 books (Karra Porter's Mad Seasons, Woolum) and a D Magazine feature (27 ppg, voted league MVP); JWA mentions only the championship.

SUPERLATIVE SCOPE HOLDS AS WRITTEN ('men's professional LEAGUE'): Tier-1 WBHOF - 'Became the first female to play in a men's professional league, signing with the Springfield Fame of the USBL in 1986' (debut June 10, 1986 vs the Staten Island Stallions), plus the Generals tour in 1987-88. Prior-claimant search: Denise Long (1969 Warriors 13th-round pick, voided by the NBA, played in a women's league instead), Lusia Harris (1977 Jazz 7th-round pick, never reported), Ann Meyers (signed with the Pacers in 1979 but was cut in camp and never played a game) - none played in a men's league. The one live hazard is Lynette Woodard, who signed with the Harlem Globetrotters in Oct 1985 and is described by some outlets as the first woman to play for a men's pro TEAM; the Globetrotters are an exhibition act, not a league, so this fact must keep the word 'league'. The 1987 Long Island Knights leg is uncited on Wikipedia but is confirmed by a 1995 Newsday report (via Spokesman-Review archive): 'The only woman to play in the USBL was ... Nancy Lieberman, who played with the Springfield Fame and the Long Island Knights.'

facts.correction: She was 38, not 39, when the WNBA tipped off: born July 1, 1958, she turned 39 nine days into the inaugural season (first game June 21, 1997) - Basketball-Reference lists her 1997 age as 38. Suggested wording: 'When the WNBA tipped off in 1997 Nancy Lieberman was 38, turning 39 nine days later, and was the league's oldest player - seventeen years after being the first pick of a professional women's league that no longer existed.'
facts.note: 'Oldest player' verified by ENUMERATION rather than assertion: pulled all eight 1997 WNBA team rosters from Basketball-Reference (106 players with birth dates) and Lieberman (b. 7/1/1958) is the oldest by more than a year, with Lynette Woodard (b. 8/12/1959) second. The Phoenix Mercury signing and the 17-year gap from the 1980 WBL first pick both check out.

facts.correction: Two superlatives need scoping. (1) 'first woman to receive a full four-year athletic scholarship at a US university' -> 'the first woman to receive a full athletic scholarship to UCLA (1974)', the wording used by all three Tier-1 halls and by UCLA itself. (2) 'first four-time All-American in women's basketball' -> 'the first four-time Kodak (collegiate) All-American, 1975-1978'. The AIAW title line is correct as written: UCLA beat Maryland 90-74 on March 25, 1978.
facts.note: PRIOR CLAIMANTS FOUND for both. Scholarship: the University of Chicago's Gertrude Dudley Scholarship (full tuition, fall 1972; first recipients Noel Bairey and Laura Silvieus), the University of Miami began awarding women's athletic scholarships in early 1973, and Wayland Baptist had scholarship women basketball players earlier still (NBC Sports, Nick Zaccardi, 2022) - so the national claim is unsupportable, while the UCLA-scoped claim is Tier-1 solid. All-American: Nera White was named an AAU All-America 15 straight years (1955-69) per the Naismith HOF, so only the COLLEGIATE/Kodak scope survives.

SUPERLATIVE HOLDS: Tier-1 WBHOF - 'the first, and only, woman to be signed to an NBA contract when she signed as a free agent with the Indiana Pacers in 1979'; Naismith HOF - 'first female player to try out with an NBA team'; Baseball HOF - 'first woman to be signed to a contract by an NBA team'. Prior-claimant search: Denise Long's 1969 Warriors pick was voided (no contract) and Lusia Harris's 1977 Jazz pick never produced a signing or a camp appearance. Two wording notes for the card: the deal is precisely a one-year, $50,000 PERSONAL-SERVICES contract that kept her in the organisation if cut (signed Sept 5, 1979; the Pacers later released her from it and she never received the full $50,000) - 'no-cut' is the popular shorthand, not the instrument; and the tryout was six practices over three days at Hinkle Fieldhouse. Her 1979-80 WBL honour is correctly stated as CO-MVP (shared with Molly Bolin of the Iowa Cornets); note WBHOF's page also claims she 'led the league in scoring', which is false - Bolin led at 32.8 ppg to Meyers' 22.2 - so do not mine that claim.

The Superstars YEARS are in unresolved conflict and no Tier-1/two-independent-Tier-2 settles it in bounded lookups. facts.correction: Drop 'first independent'. facts.note: SI (2021) does state 'first independent professional basketball league for women in the United States', but that line reproduces an old Wikipedia lead and is refuted by the ABL's own co-founder Gary Cavalli ('All previous women's basketball leagues in the U.S. had failed') and by Defector's reporting ('at least a half dozen attempts... in the previous two decades').

OPINION CLAIM, but the corpus wording ('was early on considered the better league on the floor') is honestly hedged and is directly supported by contemporaneous journalism — Seattle Times, 14 Dec 1997: 'The WNBA... according to most observers, has inferior talent compared to the ABL'; Cavalli on the day it folded: 'although we had the best product'; Val Whiting in Defector: 'I was also convinced that the better players were in the ABL'. FLAG: any question written from this fact must keep it as attributed perception ('was considered', 'observers said'), never 'the ABL was better'; the two underlying facts (signed most of the 1996 gold medalists, paid more — ABL $40k-$100k vs WNBA $15k-$50k) are separately verified.

Both figures reproduce: APBR's per-team attendance tables total 565,787 over 160 home dates in 1996-97 (avg 3,536) and 857,937 over 198 dates in 1997-98 (avg 4,333) — 4333/3536 = +22.5%, so the corpus arithmetic is right; AP/CBS News in Dec 1998 independently reported 'Year 1: 3,536 / Year 2: 4,333 (23% increase)'; the Seattle Times (Tier 1, Dec 1997) gives 3,536 for 1996-97. The 'attendance was rising when the league died' framing is supported (Seattle Times reported the league up 15.5% at the 1997-98 midpoint, though almost all of the gain was New England).

APBR's membership chronology lists exactly those eight as charter franchises, Long Beach as the 1997-98 expansion team, and Chicago Condors and Nashville Noise for 1998-99 (both confirmed as active teams by AP/CBS on the day the league folded).
